Before Gen 6, your starter's Nature was randomly decided when you received it. Saving beforehand let players soft-reset for the Nature they wanted — later softened by Mints.
EVs are gained by defeating specific Pokémon, not randomly: each species gives fixed 1-3 points (Geodude gives 1 Defense, Magikarp 1 Speed). This rule has held since Gen 1.
IVs existed from Gen 1, but capped at 15 back then (0-15). Gen 3 raised the cap to 0-31 — so a "6V" (all 31) was impossible in the originals.
Pokémon have four EXP growth rates (fast, medium, slow, and fluctuating). Mew and Pikachu are in the slow group, while Magikarp levels up extremely fast.
The Exp. Share was originally held by a single Pokémon, not shared by the party. Only from Gen 6 (X/Y) did the whole party gain half EXP, with further tweaks from Gen 7.
Friendship affects certain evolutions (Pichu → Pikachu), and also powers up Return (more friendship = more damage) and Frustration (less friendship = more damage).

Pokérus is an extremely rare beneficial condition: it doubles EV gains and can spread to the rest of your party, but the infection disappears after a few days (the doubled effect stays after being cured).
Egg Moves are inherited from the father only before Gen 6. From Gen 6 onwards, the mother can pass down Egg Moves too.
Shiny odds were 1/8192 in Gen 2, improving to 1/4096 from Gen 6. The Shiny Charm roughly doubles your odds, and chaining boosts them further.
Chaining rules differ by generation: in Let's Go, chains of 31+ greatly boost shiny odds, while in Sword/Shield chaining means battling the same species repeatedly for better rare spawns.
Pokémon size was purely visual before Scarlet/Violet, which introduced size differences shown in the wild — with no effect on battle performance.
In the catch formula, lower HP and stronger status help: Sleep or Freeze multiply the catch rate by 2, while Paralysis only by 1.5.
Quick Claw gives a 20% chance to move first. If both sides trigger it, the faster Pokémon still goes first.
Focus Band and Focus Sash differ: the Band has a 10% chance to survive any fatal hit (can trigger repeatedly), while the Sash always saves you from full HP once only.
OHKO moves (Fissure, Sheer Cold, etc.) depend on level difference: they fail if the user is lower level, and accuracy climbs with level up to a max of 30%.
Accuracy and evasion modifiers multiply, they do not add. After 6 stages of evasion boosts, the opponent's accuracy drops to roughly 33% — never a full miss.
Stat changes max out at 6 stages up or down, ±50% each. +1 Attack is ×1.5, +6 is ×4 (not ×6).
Paralysis halves Speed and gives a 25% chance of being unable to move. Freeze prevents action entirely, with only 20% thaw chance per turn (Fire moves force a thaw).
Poison hurts outside battle while walking. In battle, regular poison costs 1/8 HP per turn, while Toxic starts at 1/16 and doubles each turn.
Sleep lasts 2-4 turns. Switching while asleep keeps the sleep status on the new Pokémon — it does not wear off by switching.
Confusion gives a 33% chance to hit yourself, calculated as normal physical damage, and it can trigger recoil items like Life Orb.
Taunt lasts 3 turns and blocks status moves. Sleep Talk and Chatter can sometimes slip past the restriction.
Protect-style moves lose accuracy when used in succession: 100%, then 50%, then 25%, and so on. Feint also breaks through them.
Substitute costs 1/4 of your max HP to make a decoy. While it stands, you are immune to status and super-effective moves, but sound moves (like Boomburst) pierce it.
Baton Pass transfers stat changes, Substitute, confusion, and some item effects — but not binding moves (like Wrap) or Leech Seed.
Leech Seed drains 1/8 of the target's HP each turn. It fails on Grass types and can be bounced back by Magic Bounce.
Life Orb boosts move power by 30%, but costs 10% of your max HP after each attacking move (no HP lost if the move misses).
Choice Band/Specs/Scarf lock you into one move until you switch out.
Choice items work normally during Dynamax from Gen 8, but after Dynamax ends you are still locked into the chosen move.
Leftovers restores 1/16 max HP per turn. A Substitute doesn't get the healing, but the real Pokémon still does.
Toxic Orb and Flame Orb trigger at the end of the turn, badly poisoning or burning the holder. Magic Guard Pokémon take no damage from them.
Magic Guard blocks all indirect damage: poison, burn, sandstorm, hail, Life Orb recoil, entry hazards — but Leech Seed still drains HP (it is not a damage flag).
Multiscale halves damage taken at full HP, pairing well with Leftovers and Rest, but Mold Breaker ignores it.
Mold Breaker ignores the opponent's Ability, except defensive ones like Magic Guard and Wonder Guard, which directly affect the damage formula.
Wonder Guard (Shedinja only) blocks moves that are not super effective. Moves that don't hit it super effectively do nothing — but weather, hazards, status, and confusion self-hits still KO it.
Shedinja always has 1 HP. Leftovers heals 1/16 max HP, which rounds to 0 — so it relies on fixed healing like Rest or Soft-Boiled instead.
Shadow Tag (Wobbuffet, Gothitelle) traps the opponent, but Eject Button forces a switch anyway, and Ghost types are immune to Shadow Tag.
Sand Veil and Snow Cloak raise evasion in sandstorm/hail. Technically they lower the opponent's accuracy instead, so the math is multiplicative.
Cloud Nine temporarily removes all weather, including harsh sunlight, rain, sandstorm, hail, and the extreme weathers of Primal forms.
Weather Ball changes type with the weather: Fire in sun, Water in rain, Rock in sandstorm, Ice in hail — and its power doubles from 50 to 100.
Thunder never misses in rain, but its accuracy drops to 50% in sun, sandstorm, or hail.
Hurricane never misses in rain, but drops to 50% accuracy in sun.
Solar Beam fires in one turn under harsh sunlight with no charge, but its power is halved in rain, sandstorm, or hail.
Aurora Veil can only be used in hail, reducing physical and special damage by 1/3 for 5 turns — like a combined Reflect + Light Screen.
Gravity lasts 5 turns, grounding Flying types so they can be hit by Ground moves, and moves like Fly and Sky Drop become unusable.
Trick Room lasts 5 turns and makes slower Pokémon move first. Priority moves still follow their own order (a +1 priority still beats a normal move).
Trick Room's Chinese name differs between regions — in English it is simply "Trick Room", reversing speed order.
Tailwind lasts 4 turns and doubles your side's Speed, but items like Lagging Tail and halved-Speed effects are unaffected.
Sticky Hold (Grimer family) protects your item from Thief, Trick, and similar — but Knock Off still removes the item and deals damage.
Thief and Snatch cannot steal Big Root or Life Orb, which count as special items.
Prankster (Murkrow) lets status moves go first, but only status moves — attacking moves are unaffected.
Speed Boost (Blaziken) raises Speed by 1 stage at the end of each turn, up to +6. Pairing it with Protect and Baton Pass is a classic strategy.
Download (Porygon) boosts Attack or Sp. Atk based on the opponent's lower defensive stat (Defense or Sp. Def) — it raises the attacking stat that hits their weaker side.
Trace (Porygon2) copies the opponent's Ability on entry, but copying unstable Abilities like Imposter does not work.
Synchronize (Abra) gives wild Pokémon a 50% chance to share your Nature — a trick players use to hunt specific legendary Natures.
Magnet Pull (Magnemite) attracts wild Steel types, greatly boosting your encounter rate in the right area.
Lightning Rod (Manectric) absorbs all Electric moves and raises Sp. Atk by 1 stage. In doubles, an ally's Electric move aimed elsewhere gets drawn to it too.
Storm Drain (Water types) absorbs all Water moves and raises Sp. Atk by 1 stage — the Water version of Lightning Rod.
Sap Sipper absorbs all Grass moves and raises Attack by 1 stage, even turning Leech Seed into an Attack boost.
Flash Fire (Arcanine) absorbs all Fire moves, and afterwards your own Fire moves deal 1.5× damage, with full Fire immunity.
Water Absorb (Quagsire) absorbs all Water moves and heals 1/4 of max HP — full Water immunity plus healing.
Dry Skin (Parasect) heals HP in rain and loses HP in sun. Water moves heal it, but Fire moves deal 1.25× damage.
Limber (Ditto) prevents paralysis. If Ditto transforms, Limber is lost — it copies the target's Ability instead.
Sturdy (Geodude) survives any OHKO move at full HP with 1 HP left, but only when HP is full.
Rock Head (Onix) prevents recoil damage, so Double-Edge and Brave Bird cost nothing.
Rock Head and Reckless (Staraptor) are different: Reckless boosts recoil moves by 20%, while Rock Head negates the recoil entirely.
Sheer Force (Nidoking) boosts moves with secondary effects by 30%, but the secondary effects (paralysis, burn, flinch, etc.) no longer trigger.
Huge Power (Azumarill) doubles physical attack damage — calculated as ×2 on the final damage, not the stat itself.
Pure Power (Medicham) works exactly like Huge Power, doubling final physical damage.
Unaware (Quagsire) ignores the opponent's stat changes on both offense and defense — a +6 Attack opponent hits you as if it were 0.
Defiant (Braviary) raises Attack by 2 stages whenever any stat is lowered — an Intimidate on you becomes a free +2 Attack.
Competitive (Gardevoir) is like Defiant but raises Sp. Atk by 2 stages instead.
Contrary (Serperior) inverts stat changes: Dragon Dance would lower Attack and Speed, while Leaf Storm's drop becomes a Sp. Atk boost.
Own Tempo (Slowbro) prevents confusion. Swagger still raises the opponent's Attack, but the confusion is ignored.
Oblivious (Slowpoke) blocks infatuation and Captivate, but not Taunt — it only protects against the infatuation family of effects.
Swift Swim (Kingdra) doubles Speed in rain — a staple of rain teams.
Chlorophyll (Venusaur) doubles Speed in harsh sunlight, pairing beautifully with Solar Beam.
Sand Rush (Excadrill) doubles Speed in sandstorm — a core of sand teams.
Ice Scales (Snom) doubles Sp. Def in hail, though hail's chip damage makes it awkward in practice.
Drought (Groudon) and Drizzle (Kyogre) set permanent weather on entry, lasting until the setter switches out or faints.
Desolate Land and Primordial Sea (Primal Groudon/Kyogre) create extreme weathers that ordinary weather cannot override — only the opposing extreme weather can replace them.
Delta Stream (Mega Rayquaza) creates strong winds that remove Flying's weaknesses, so Flying types take neutral damage from Ice, Rock, and Electric.
Illusion (Zoroark) disguises you as the last Pokémon in your party. Taking a hit breaks the illusion.
Transform (Ditto, Mew) copies all stat changes, Ability, and moves — but not HP, IVs, or EVs.
Copycat (Meowth) uses the target's last move, but you must be able to learn that move yourself.
Mimic (Mr. Mime) copies the target's last move, permanently replacing one of your move slots until the battle ends or you relearn.
Chatter (Chatot) uses the target's last move, but copied attacking moves deal half damage.
Sleep Talk (Snorlax) lets you use a random move you know while asleep — including Rest itself, though using Rest this way doesn't wake you.
Snore (Snorlax) can only be used while asleep, has fixed 50 power, and can partially bypass Protect (a chance to hit).
Snatch (Electrode) steals the opponent's healing or boosting moves like Rest, Dragon Dance, or Swords Dance — but not Substitute or Baton Pass.
Trick and Switch moves swap items, but fail against Sticky Hold, Mega Stones, or Z-Crystals.
Knock Off's power rose from 20 to 65 from Gen 8, and it deals even more damage when removing the opponent's item (up to 97.5).
Thief's power changed from 40 to 60 from Gen 4, keeping the steal effect only if you hold no item.
Covet (Skitty) steals the opponent's item, but only if you hold nothing and their item is stealable.
Recycle (Grimer) restores a used or thrown item — even a Berry you flung with Fling.
Fling's power depends on the item thrown: Life Orb is 70, Choice Band 80, King's Rock 100.
Natural Gift's power depends on the held Berry, e.g. Oran Berry gives 60, Sitrus Berry gives 80, with the type also varying by Berry.
Before Gen 4, Berries only healed HP or cured status. From Gen 4 they gained damage-halving and stat-boosting effects.
Salac and Petaya Berries raise Speed or Sp. Atk when HP falls below 1/4, but the trigger is harsh, so they rarely see use.
Bright Powder lowers the opponent's accuracy by 10% — a separate multiplier, not additive.
Wide Lens boosts move accuracy by 10%: Hypnosis goes from 60% to 66%.
Zoom Lens boosts accuracy by 20% when you move after the opponent — no effect if you are faster.
Quick Claw and Lagging Tail cancel out when held together: the Tail's guaranteed last-move beats the Claw's 20% first-move.
Eject Button forces a switch when you are hit, and it works even against Shadow Tag.
Red Card forces the attacker out when you are hit, but fails against Suction Cups (Octillery).
Weakness Policy raises Attack and Sp. Atk by 2 stages when hit super effectively, then the item is consumed — one use only.
Assault Vest boosts Sp. Def by 50%, but you cannot use status moves while holding it.
Eviolite boosts Defense and Sp. Def by 50% if the holder can still evolve — making pre-evolutions like Chansey and Scyther surprisingly bulky.
Everstone blocks evolution, and in breeding it guarantees the offspring inherits the holder's Nature (from Gen 6, 100% inheritance).
Destiny Knot passes down 5 of the parents' combined 12 IVs when breeding — a huge boost to breeding 6V eggs.
The Power items (Weight, Bracer, Belt, Lens, Band, Anklet) cut Speed (the Weight does) but guarantee the matching stat's EV gain, plus 8 extra EVs per battle.
Macho Brace doubles EV gains at the cost of Speed, similar to the Power items.
PC box sorting works differently across games: Sword/Shield lets you sort by individual IVs, making it easy to find high-IV Pokémon.
Marking lets you tag IVs with symbols like triangles and hearts. Many players use 6 marks to note perfect IVs in HP, Attack, Defense, Sp. Atk, Sp. Def, and Speed.
Bulk release only arrived in X/Y. Before that, you had to release Pokémon one by one.
The GTS debuted in Diamond/Pearl, letting players deposit Pokémon online and trade for what they wanted.
Wonder Trade debuted in X/Y, randomly trading with players worldwide. It later inspired the Wonder Box in Pokémon HOME.
Horde battles existed in X/Y and ORAS, spawning 5 Pokémon at once in grass, and could be forced with Sweet Scent.
In X/Y, chaining is done with the Poké Radar: defeating the same species repeatedly in grass raises the odds of high IVs and shinies.
Island Scan in Sun/Moon works by scanning 10 QR codes a day, spawning rare Pokémon (like starters) in set areas.
Scarlet/Violet is the first game with a truly enterable school. Earlier Pokémon schools were only dialogue scenes — Paldea's academy is fully explorable.
Picnics replaced camping in Scarlet/Violet. You can breed, wash, and make sandwiches, which boost encounter odds for specific types.
Sandwich powers in Scarlet/Violet include Encounter, Catching, Item Drop, and EXP boosts — each tied to a type, lasting 30 minutes.
Terastallizing appears in Tera Raids in the wild. Defeating them drops Tera Shards used to change a Pokémon's Tera type.
Flying in Scarlet/Violet no longer needs a field move — just open the map and fast travel directly.
The HM system was removed in Gen 8 (Sword/Shield). No more Surf or Fly slaves; instead you get the bike and the Flying Taxi.
The bicycle has been essential since Gen 1, but speeds differ: Gold/Silver had the Mach Bike and Acro Bike modes.
Running shoes didn't exist in Red/Blue/Green — they first appeared in Gen 3 (Ruby/Sapphire), letting you run with the B button.
Sweet Scent instantly triggers a wild battle when used in grass, caves, or water — a great tool for shiny hunting and chaining.
Repel avoids wild Pokémon at or below the level of your lead Pokémon, but it doesn't work on special encounters or fishing.
Fishing mechanics differ by generation: in Gens 1-2 you pick a rod after an encounter; from Gen 3 you reel in with the A button timing.
Pokémon cries have no battle effect whatsoever — purely visual and audio flavor.
Double battles were introduced in Gen 3 (Ruby/Sapphire). The first two generations were single battles only.
Triple battles debuted in Gen 5 (Black/White), appearing only in select areas and online play.
Rotation battles arrived with Gen 5's triple battles, rotating three Pokémon on a wheel — but they were removed in later games.
Inverse battles appear at the Inverse Mountain in Black/White, fully inverting type matchups — Fire hits Water super effectively.
Battle Royal debuted in Sun/Moon: four players, one Pokémon each, scoring by knockouts and surviving to the end.
Max Raid Battles debuted in Sword/Shield: four players battle one Dynamax Pokémon and can catch it after winning.
Tera Raid Battles replaced Max Raids in Scarlet/Violet — similar mechanics, but with Terastallized Pokémon and type twists.
The Battle Tower has been a staple since Crystal (Gen 2), with each generation adding similar facilities like the Battle Frontier and Battle Tree.
The Battle Tree in Sun/Moon offers singles, doubles, and multiplayer, with cameo opponents like Cynthia and Brock.
The Battle Frontier in Emerald and Platinum is the most complex battle facility collection, featuring the Battle Pyramid, Battle Factory, and Battle Palace.
In the Battle Factory, you can't use your own Pokémon — you rent provided ones and can swap after each round.
In the Battle Palace, you don't control your Pokémon directly — they choose to attack, defend, or dodge based on their Nature. Pure luck.
In the Battle Pyramid, you explore a maze on foot with no items (except at rest points) and no auto-healing after battles.
The Battle Roulette in Platinum spins a roulette each round, adding random battle rules like weather or status conditions — pure luck.
The Pokéwalker linked with HeartGold/SoulSilver: transfer a Pokémon to the pedometer and earn EXP and items by walking in real life.
Pokéblocks in Ruby/Sapphire raise a Pokémon's Cuteness for Contests, but have zero effect in battle.
Contests existed in Gens 3-4 (Ruby/Sapphire and Diamond/Pearl/Platinum) as a fully separate show system, scoring moves and appearance.
The Pokémon Musical in Black/White lets you arrange Pokémon cries into music — pure casual fun.
Pokéstar Studios in Black 2/White 2 lets you film Pokémon movies, with different scripts and moves affecting the ending.
Amity Square in Diamond/Pearl is a Pokétch minigame where you walk your Pokémon on the touchscreen to raise friendship.
Pokémon-Amie debuted in X/Y: pet your Pokémon on the touchscreen to raise affection, with reactions varying by Nature.
Washing in Scarlet/Violet picnics uses soap to clean Pokémon, making them sparkle (and raising friendship).
Pokémon Camp replaced Amie in Sword/Shield: set up tents and cook curry, whose quality affects how much your team recovers.
Curry in Sword/Shield comes in ordinary, tasty, and Charizard-class grades. Better curry restores more HP and PP and can cure status.
Pokémon cries were heavily compressed in Gens 1-2 due to cartridge limits, with audio quality improving from Gen 3.
Pokémon gender ratios are fixed per species: Eevee is 87.5% male, 12.5% female, while Pikachu is 50/50.
Height and weight are recorded in the Pokédex, but they don't affect battle — except for Grass Knot and Heat Crash, which scale with weight.
Grass Knot's power scales with the target's weight: the heavier the target, the higher the power (max 120, min 40).
Heat Crash's power scales with the weight ratio between user and target: heavier users hit harder (max 120).
Heat Wave gains accuracy in harsh sunlight (90% to 100%), but its power doesn't change.
Hydro Pump and Fire Blast are not affected by weather. Only a few moves, like Thunder, Hurricane, and Solar Beam, change with weather.
Hidden Power's type and power depend on the user's IVs. Before Gen 6, its power ranged 30-70 with the type set by IVs.
Hidden Power is the official English name (the Chinese name differs by region): from Gen 5 its power is fixed at 60, with the type still determined by IVs.
Hidden Power's type formula is complex — players use calculators to predict it, and from Gen 7 an NPC judge can check its type.
TMs were single-use in Gen 1, disappearing after use. They became reusable from Gen 5.
In Gen 8, TMs split into reusable TMs and single-use TRs (Technical Records).
TRs debuted in Sword/Shield, obtained from Max Raid Battles. They vanish after one use but can be farmed repeatedly.
Move Tutors appear in every generation, teaching moves in exchange for Heart Scales or Shards.
Heart Scales first appeared in Gen 3 (Ruby/Sapphire) for relearning forgotten moves, and became a staple item ever since.
Shards in Black/White are used for move tutoring, coming in red, blue, green, and yellow, each tied to different move types.
Battle Points (BP) are earned in battle facilities and spent on rare items like Life Orb, Choice Band, and Eviolite.
In Sword/Shield, BP comes from Max Raids and the Battle Tower; in earlier games, only the Battle Tower gave BP.
Ribbons debuted in X/Y, awarded for achievements like beating the game or maxing friendship, and are shown in battle.
From Gen 8, Ribbons can be viewed in the PC box. Some are very rare, like the Master Rank Ribbon for a 50-win Battle Tower streak.
Nicknames in Gen 1 were limited to 5 characters, expanded to 6 in Gen 2 and 10 from Gen 3 (varies by language).
Nicknames can't be changed after trading — only the original trainer can rename a Pokémon, a rule held since Gen 1.
Each Pokémon's ID number is generated at creation, distinguishing it from other trainers' Pokémon. After trading, the ID changes to the new trainer's.
The hidden ID determines shininess, gender, and Nature. It's a 32-bit random value combined with trainer IDs for shiny odds.
In Gen 2, shininess used a simple check: specific stats (Defense, Speed, etc.) had to equal 10. From Gen 3, PID-based calculation took over.
From Gen 6, chaining raises shiny odds: defeating the same species repeatedly pushes the shiny rate much higher.
When breeding from Gen 7 (Sun/Moon), the offspring inherits the mother's Poké Ball type.
Sword/Shield added new ball types like the Sport Ball and special balls with unique looks and catch effects.
The Master Ball appears only once per game (except special distributions) — it has the highest catch rate and never fails.
The Timer Ball improves with each passing turn, reaching 4× catch rate from turn 10 onward.
The Dusk Ball works better at night or in caves, with a 3× catch rate in those conditions.
The Dive Ball works better underwater — in Ruby/Sapphire's underwater caves its effect doubles.
The Nest Ball works better on low-level Pokémon: the lower the level, the higher the catch rate (up to 3×).
The Heal Ball fully restores HP and status of the caught Pokémon — handy if you want to use it right away.
The Luxury Ball makes caught Pokémon gain friendship faster, though it doesn't add friendship directly.
The Premier Ball has no special effect — just a different look, obtained as a bonus when buying Poké Balls in bulk.
The number of shakes isn't random — it's set by the catch rate. Higher catch rate means fewer shakes (3 is the usual success).
Fleeing in the wild works better if you're faster, but trapping moves like Block and Spider Web prevent escape.
You can't flee from story battles (Gym Leaders, Elite Four, legendaries) — only switch Pokémon instead.
A fainted Pokémon can't be switched in — revive it first with a Revive or Max Revive.
Pokémon Centers heal for free in every generation — always feel free to head back and resupply.
PC boxes store Pokémon: early games held only 120, later expanded to hundreds or thousands.
In Sword/Shield, the box can be accessed anytime via the Switch home button — but not during battle.
The Lucky Egg boosts EXP gained by 50% when held — usually obtained later in the game.
Before Sword/Shield's launch, Game Freak announced it would not include all National Dex Pokémon — the first mainline cut, sparking global outrage known as "Dexit".
After Dexit, players trended #BringBackNationalDex on Twitter, topping global trends for weeks — but the decision never changed.
Scarlet/Violet launched with severe performance issues, constant frame drops and stuttering. Players called it "PowerPoint Pokémon"; patches helped but problems remain.
On Scarlet/Violet's launch day, a duplication glitch let players copy items and Pokémon before it was quickly patched.
Brilliant Diamond/Shining Pearl's chibi art style drew criticism, nicknamed "Pokémon chocolate beans" versus the original 2006 game's serious look.
Legends: Arceus was hyped as a revolutionary entry — and delivered, with overhauled battle and catching systems, dubbed "Pokémon Breath of the Wild".
Sword/Shield's DLC was the series' first paid expansion (Isle of Armor, Crown Tundra), replacing the old enhanced-version model like Emerald and Platinum.
Ultra Sun/Moon is called the laziest enhanced version: minimal additions over Sun/Moon and nearly identical story — "selling the same game twice".
ORAS removed the Battle Frontier, replacing it with the Battle Resort — a decision that upset long-time fans.
HeartGold/SoulSilver is widely considered the best remake: all the original content plus following Pokémon, Pokéwalker, and more.
Black/White was the first to explore human-Pokémon relationships deeply — N's "liberate Pokémon" ideology sparked real philosophical debate.
X/Y was the first fully 3D mainline entry — Black/White had 3D scenes, but X/Y brought full 3D models and camera rotation.
Sun/Moon replaced the Gym Challenge with the Island Challenge (Island Kahunas) — the first mainline game to remove Gyms.
Sword/Shield's Gym battles added a cheering crowd that randomly boosts your Pokémon — jokingly called the "hype squad".
Scarlet/Violet is the first true open world, with three storylines (Victory Road, Starfall Street, Path of Legends) playable in any order.
Scarlet/Violet added Auto Battle (Let's Go!): send out a Pokémon to auto-fight wilds — the first semi-automated grinding mechanic.
Terastallization was mocked at reveal ("a crystal on the head?") but its strategic depth won players over after release.
Scarlet/Violet's Area Zero is called the darkest story in the series — time paradoxes, clones, and an AI professor, a huge contrast to the series' usual tone.
Arven's storyline (Path of Legends) is called the most touching side story, centered on his bond with the injured Mabosstiff — many players cried.
The Teal Mask and Indigo Disk DLC added Kitakami and Blueberry Academy, whose battle system is praised as the series' best battle content.
"Groudon can't fly" started from the anime movie Destiny Deoxys, and became one of the most famous memes through endless photoshops and jokes.
The Chinese nickname "Fatty" for Dragonite comes from a mistranslation in early pirated copies — the Japanese name Kairyu's similarity to a Chinese phrase.
"King of One" is the community's tease for Flareon: in early games its Attack was high but Fire moves were special, leaving it unable to use that power.
"God of One" teases Entei, whose shallow early movepool left it with great stats but few good moves — all looks, little substance.
"Toilet King" teases Regigigas: its Slow Start halves Attack and Speed for 5 turns — "as slow as a toilet".
"Dragon Slayer" is Azumarill's title: Huge Power doubles its physical damage, letting Play Rough easily crush Dragon types (even Rayquaza).
"Universe No.1 Incineroar" teases Incineroar's dominance in Sun/Moon and Sword/Shield competitive play, with sky-high usage rates.
Incineroar stays strong in Scarlet/Violet — "the eternal Tiger God": nerfed repeatedly, but Intimidate + Fake Out + Flare Blitz remains a competitive staple.
"E-sports Pokémon" teases Porygon-Z: it looks like a glitchy 3D model and evolves by leveling up with a Dubious Disc — like applying a patch.
Amoonguss is called "Shroom Shield" in doubles: Rage Powder draws every single-target move, and 100%-accuracy Spore makes it a top controller.
Pachirisu made history at the 2014 VGC World Championship: with Follow Me, Protect, and Nuzzle support, it helped Se Jun Park win — the "White Devil".
Lapras is hated in Sword/Shield Max Raids for Perish Song: if your team's damage is too low, everyone faints in three turns — the "party wipe engine".
Magikarp is joked as the weakest Pokémon, but its evolution Gyarados is a competitive staple — hence the "hidden boss" meme.
Slowpoke's evolution (a Shellder biting its tail) is called the most bizarre evolution, sparking the community debate "does it hurt?"
Ditto is called the "universal plug": it can breed with any breedable Pokémon (except legendaries and the undiscovered egg group).
A classic Zoroark play: disguise as a Fighting-weak Pokémon like Blissey to bait a Fighting move — then laugh because Zoroark is Dark and immune to Fighting's synergy bait.
Shedinja is the "1HP God": Wonder Guard blocks everything except super-effective moves, and with Protect and status immunity it's one of a kind.
Wobbuffet is the "double-edged sword": Shadow Tag plus Counter/Mirror Coat can revenge-kill, but a good read lets the opponent set up freely.
Blissey's pre-evolution Chansey is the "pink wall": base 250 HP plus Eviolite, Soft-Boiled, and Toxic makes it the core of stall teams.
Blissey is Chansey's evolution, yet Chansey + Eviolite is bulkier in battle, since Eviolite grants 50% defenses to unevolved Pokémon.
Lucario became a fan favorite after Diamond/Pearl, and Game Freak pushed it as the "Aura hero", even adding it to Super Smash Bros.
Greninja became a superstar after X/Y thanks to Protean and its cool design, winning the 2016 Pokémon general election and earning a special form.
Greninja returned in the Indigo Disk DLC with Protean restored — but nerfed to once per battle. Old fans teared up; the power is gone.
Mimikyu's tragic backstory and cute design made it a hit after Sun/Moon, inspiring fan works and becoming one of Gen 7's most beloved Pokémon.
Mimikyu comes from "Mimic" + "kyu" (Japanese for Q). Its design is inspired by Pikachu fan art — Game Freak calls it the most Pikachu-like Pokémon.
Toxtricity's Punk Rock ability boosts sound moves. Players pair it with Boomburst and Choice Specs for the "sound cannon" build.
Toxel, Toxtricity's baby form, burps during Pokémon Camp interactions — a detail fans praised as "the devs know what's cute".
Rockruff evolves into different Lycanroc forms by version: Midday in Sun, Midnight in Moon, and Dusk added in Ultra Sun/Moon.
Dusk Form Lycanroc needs a strict evolution: in Ultra Sun/Moon, level up Rockruff between 5:00-5:59 PM real time.
Komala is always asleep — its Comatose ability keeps it in permanent sleep, but it's immune to moves like Hypnosis.
Morelull's sleepy mushroom design made it the "most huggable Pokémon", appearing early in Lush Jungle and melting players' hearts.
Buzzwole's muscle-bound look earned it "the gym coach of the Pokémon world", with an Ultra Beast lore of being too muscular to move fast.
Pheromosa is the "glass cannon": 151 base Speed and 137 Attack, but only 37 Defense — "win or lose in an instant".
Xurkitree has 173 base Sp. Atk — the highest among non-legendary Pokémon, earning it "the special cannon".
Nihilego is "the slime of the Pokémon world": a transparent body showing its inner core, inspired by jellyfish.
Guzzlord's planet-eating lore earned it "the Thanos of Pokémon": an Ultra Beast with an endless appetite that devours everything.
Necrozma can fuse into Dusk Mane and Dawn Wings in Ultra Sun/Moon, reaching 680 base stats and able to separate — "the Transformer of Pokémon".
Ultra Necrozma transforms via Ultra Burst in battle, with a spectacular animation — "the Super Saiyan transformation of Pokémon".
Zeraora debuted as an event Pokémon in Ultra Sun/Moon, looking like The Flash with 143 base Speed — "the Flash of Pokémon".
Meltan debuted in Pokémon GO before transferring to Let's Go — the first Pokémon to premiere in a mobile game and then join the main series.
Melmetal, Meltan's evolution, is the first Steel/Fighting mythical, requiring 400 candies to evolve in Pokémon GO.
Zarude appeared in the Isle of Armor DLC, inspired by a jungle wild man, with Defiant plus Close Combat as a physical threat.
Zarude starred in the movie Pokémon: Secrets of the Jungle — the first mythical distributed during a movie's theatrical run.
Zacian and Zamazenta are legendary heroes in Sword/Shield lore, with Crowned forms that require their signature items in battle.
Eternatus is the source of Dynamax in Sword/Shield, and its Eternamax form is the largest Pokémon ever (filling the whole screen).
Calyrex appeared in the Crown Tundra DLC, fusing into Ice Rider and Shadow Rider with 680 base stats and the As One ability.
Calyrex's backstory is an ancient king who can control humans — joked as "the tyrant of the Pokémon world".
Paldea's starters — Sprigatito, Fuecoco, Quaxly — sparked huge "which one?" debates. Fuecoco's goofy charm won fans, while Sprigatito's final form Meowscarada gained many admirers.
Meowscarada became a top physical attacker thanks to Flower Trick, a move that always crits — "the Grass-type war god".
Skeledirge's signature move Torch Song raises Sp. Atk, pairing with Sing for the "sleep-kill" strategy — the poster child of slow cannons.
Quaquaval's rare Water/Fighting typing and Moxie-like Dancer ability let it copy the opponent's Dragon Dance in doubles.
Koraidon and Miraidon are Scarlet/Violet's box legendaries, transforming in battle with field effects from their Orichalcum Pulse and Hadron Engine abilities.
Koraidon is jokingly called "the motorcycle lizard": it turns into a ride Pokémon in Scarlet/Violet, sprinting across the wild like a red motorbike.
Miraidon is "the electronic lizard": its ride form looks like a purple electric motorcycle with glowing circuits.
Terastallization's look was mocked as "a crystal chandelier on the head", but the type-changing mechanic became the new core of competitive play.
Tera Raids are called "grinding pits": high-star raids drop Herba Mystica for master sandwiches that boost shiny odds — the core of endgame.
Tera Raids occasionally spawn shiny Tera Pokémon, with high shiny odds (around 1/200 with the Shiny Charm) — "the most generous shiny hunting".
The Teal Mask DLC's Kitakami story features Ogerpon, a masked ogre with Grass/Water/Fire/Rock form switching — "the Kamen Rider of Pokémon".
Ogerpon's four masks correspond to the four seasons, unlocked through the Festival of Masks quest.
Terapagos is the core legendary of the Indigo Disk DLC, with a stunning cosmic Stellar Form — "the cosmic overlord of Pokémon".
Terapagos' Tera Shift ability turns its Terastallization into the Stellar Form, granting resistance to all types — absurdly strong.
Area Zero holds Paradox Pokémon: Ancient forms (Roaring Moon, Great Tusk) and Future forms (Iron Hands, Iron Jugulis), inspired by sci-fi timelines.
Roaring Moon is an Ancient Paradox in Scarlet, resembling a prehistoric Salamence — "the dinosaur of Pokémon".
Iron Hands is a Future Paradox in Violet, a robotic Hariyama — "the Terminator of Pokémon".
Scarlet/Violet's official online tournaments were delayed repeatedly by server issues — players joked the game should be "Pokémon Disconnect/Violet".
The complex Terastallization mechanic made the competitive meta "bloom": players joke every Pokémon can become whatever type it wants.
In doubles, fast Normal-Tera Pokémon using Extreme Speed is common — the "Tera Extreme Speed team", a mainstream meta build.
The Item Printer in the Blueberry Academy's economy class exchanges LP for items, including Bottle Caps — very convenient.
Golden Bottle Caps in Scarlet/Violet come from Tera Raids and school classes, drastically lowering the barrier to 6V training — praised as the friendliest training ever.
The Mirror Herb in Scarlet/Violet copies the opponent's stat boosts in battle, enabling the classic "counter-boost" strategy.
Ability Patches in Scarlet/Violet can change a Pokémon's Ability to its Hidden Ability — previously only via breeding or events.
Mints in Scarlet/Violet change a Pokémon's stat modifiers: the Nature's name stays, but an Adamant Mint makes it boost Attack and lower Sp. Atk.
Vitamins in Scarlet/Violet directly raise EVs, but each caps at 100 points per stat — beyond that, only Feathers or battles can continue raising them.
In Scarlet/Violet breeding, if a parent holds the Destiny Knot, the child inherits 5 of the parents' 12 combined IVs, with the last one random — the core of 6V breeding.
In Scarlet/Violet picnic breeding, compatible egg-group Pokémon in the picnic will produce eggs — but only male+female, male+Ditto, or female+Ditto combos.
During picnics, Pokémon chat with each other and sometimes mention their trainer's quirks — "your trainer is a foodie" and other cute lines.
In picnics, wash your Pokémon enough and they sparkle — not a shiny, but the clean effect at 100% cleanliness.
On the Scarlet/Violet map, flying from Area Zero sends you to its entrance — you can't fly deeper inside and must walk.
Scarlet/Violet's story runs three simultaneous paths — Victory Road, Starfall Street, and Path of Legends — each with its own characters and emotional arcs.
Last but not least: in 2023, Game Freak announced the Pokémon series has shipped over 480 million copies — beating Super Mario and Tetris to become the best-selling game series ever.
For your starter, pick the one you like most — don't be swayed by "strength". No main-story fight has a power gate, and any starter clears the game. Love your pick.

Early on, catch around 6 Pokémon of different types for variety. Don't push through with only your starter — a bad matchup will hurt. Common early finds like Geodude, Caterpie, and Pidgey are all usable.
If you meet a shiny, catch it no matter what. Base odds are 1/4096 — even if it's weak or hard to catch, throw your best balls. Many veterans go hundreds of hours without one.
Money is tight early on — don't hoard Poké Balls mindlessly. Prioritize Potions and Poké Balls over situational cures like Paralyze Heal or Ice Heal, which you may never need.
Every town's Pokémon Center heals for free. Don't burn Potions outside — just head back to the Center to resupply.
Every town has NPCs giving away items. Talk to everyone — you'll get free Balls, Potions, and Berries, saving a lot of money.
EXP is precious early on — let all your Pokémon battle. Training only your starter means a rough time when you hit a Gym that counters it.
Once you get the Exp. Share, give it to your lowest-level Pokémon. It gains EXP without battling, keeping your team even.
Don't waste TMs early. Before Gen 8, TMs were single-use — save them until you're sure a Pokémon needs the move.
Keep HM users handy early on. Surf and Fly need specific Pokémon in your party — don't box them, or you can't explore.
Type matchups are the most important battle mechanic: super effective = ×2 damage, resisted = ×0.5, immune = ×0. Learning the type chart is the first lesson.
The easiest loop to memorize: Fire → Grass → Water → Fire. The basic triangle, visible from the very first starters.
Normal-type moves hit nothing super effectively. They're resisted (×0.5) by Rock and Steel, and completely blocked by Ghost — never use Normal moves on Ghosts.
Ghost types are immune to Normal and Fighting moves. If your Pokémon only knows Normal moves, a Ghost Gym will be painful.
Dragon only hits Dragon super effectively. Dragon moves are resisted by Steel (×0.5) — Dragon is not an all-purpose type.
Fairy is immune to Dragon moves. Bring a Fairy-type to a Dragon Gym and the fight becomes trivial.
Steel is immune to Poison moves — your best pick for Poison Gyms.
Ground is immune to Electric moves. Against an Electric Gym, Ground types (Geodude, Sandshrew) make Electric attacks useless.
Flying is immune to Ground moves. Never use Ground attacks against Flying types.
Psychic is weak to Ghost and Dark. A Psychic team against a Dark Gym will suffer.
Dark and Ghost don't counter each other symmetrically: Dark hits Ghost super effectively, but Ghost hits Dark resisted (×0.5). Use Fighting or Fairy against Dark instead.
Fighting hits Normal, Rock, Steel, Ice, and Dark super effectively — very useful for the main story, covering many Gyms.
Bug hits Grass, Psychic, and Dark super effectively, but Bug Pokémon often lack late-game power — not a recommended main team member.
Poison hits Grass and Fairy super effectively — a Grass Gym becomes easy with a Poison type.
Rock hits Flying, Bug, Fire, and Ice super effectively — a great helper against Flying Gyms.
Ice hits Grass, Ground, Flying, and Dragon super effectively. Ice is one of only two Dragon counters (the other is Fairy) — very strong for Dragon Gyms.
Ground hits Fire, Electric, Poison, Rock, and Steel super effectively — one of the widest offensive type coverages, very practical.
Water hits Fire, Ground, and Rock super effectively — your best friend for Fire Gyms.
Grass hits Water, Ground, and Rock super effectively — very effective for Water Gyms.
Fire hits Grass, Ice, Bug, and Steel super effectively — a great helper for Grass and Ice Gyms.
Electric hits Water and Flying super effectively — very effective for Water Gyms (but remember Ground is immune to Electric).
Psychic hits Poison and Fighting super effectively — very strong for Fighting Gyms.
Dark hits Psychic and Ghost super effectively — your best choice for Psychic Gyms.
Steel hits Ice, Rock, and Fairy super effectively — very effective for Fairy Gyms.
Fairy hits Fighting, Dragon, and Dark super effectively — a great helper for Dragon and Fighting Gyms.
Dual-type weaknesses stack: Charizard (Fire/Flying) hit by Rock takes ×2 for Fire and ×2 for Flying = ×4 damage. That's the origin of the famous 4× Rock weakness.
Dual-type resistances stack too: Ferrothorn (Grass/Steel) hit by Grass takes ×0.5 (Steel resists) ×0.5 (Grass resists) = ×0.25 — a quadruple resist.
Immunity beats resistance: Ground is fully immune to Electric — zero damage, no calculation needed. Immunity is your greatest advantage in battle.
Don't ignore status moves. Swords Dance gives +2 Attack (×2 damage) — one turn of setup doubles your next two attacks. Tremendous strategic value.
Protect-style moves are the most critical defense: they block an attack entirely. In doubles, using Protect to cover your partner is a classic play.
You don't need to understand IVs and EVs to beat the main story. Those are for competitive players — newcomers only need levels and type matchups.
If EVs interest you, remember one thing: different Pokémon give different EVs. Geodude gives Defense, Magikarp gives Speed, Ralts gives Sp. Atk.
EVs cap at 252 per stat and 510 total. You can't max everything — physical attackers usually run 252 Attack / 252 Speed / 4 HP.
IVs aren't shown as numbers in-game — the judge gives rough ratings. "This Pokémon's HP is fantastic" means that IV is around 31. Breeding 6V is endgame content.
Natures modify stats: +10% to one, -10% to another. Adamant boosts Attack and lowers Sp. Atk (physical attacker); Timid boosts Speed and lowers Attack (fast special attacker).
You don't need to hunt Natures for the main story — the difficulty is low, and any Nature clears the game. Save Nature training for competitive play.
Friendship affects certain evolutions (Pichu → Pikachu) and Return's power. Walk with your Pokémon, battle, and heal them — friendship rises naturally.
Level advantage is the simplest way to clear the game. Stuck at a Gym? Grind 10 levels above the leader and push through with type advantage.
Late-game EXP comes fast from battles and EXP Candies. Candies, introduced in Sword/Shield, boost levels quickly and are extremely convenient.
Your starter choice barely matters — the strength gap between starters is far smaller than you imagine. Pick your favorite; love beats stats.
To make the run easier: Water starters are usually the safest (few weaknesses), Grass starters struggle early (many Gyms resist Grass), and Fire starters hit their stride mid-game.
Don't train only one Pokémon. Many newcomers over-rely on their starter, then hit a wall at a bad type matchup. Raise at least 3-4 different types.
Keep at least one Pokémon per common attacking type. A balanced team covering Fire, Water, Grass, Electric, Ground, and Fighting avoids being walled by any single Gym.
Don't look down on common wild Pokémon. Early birds (Fletchling, Taillow) and bugs (Caterpie, Grubbin) become strong after evolving — don't abandon them for being weak early.
Before a Gym challenge, check the Gym's type. Preparing a counter in advance makes the fight far easier — grab a Fire or Flying type before a Grass Gym.
Level advantage is the most reliable strategy. Can't beat a Gym? Grind 5-10 levels in the grass and the matchup stops mattering.
HM moves need a "HM slave" — don't waste moveslots on your main team. Catch a dedicated carrier (Bibarel, Tropius) and teach it all the HMs.
From Gen 8 (Sword/Shield) onward, HMs are gone — no more HM slaves. Use the Flying Taxi or bike instead. Watch for version differences.
Repel is your exploration best friend. Tired of low-level wilds? A spray avoids encounters as long as your lead is higher level.
Sweet Scent actively draws wilds. To hunt a specific Pokémon or grind, use it in grass to trigger battles instantly — much faster than walking around.
Store spare Pokémon in the PC. Anything you're not using goes into the box, freeing party slots, and you can withdraw them anytime.
Catching duplicates pays off: pick the best IVs, trade spares for rewards (like LP in Scarlet/Violet), and some versions need Pokédex completion for bonuses.
Don't sell evolution stones carelessly. Fire, Thunder, and Water Stones are scarce until late game — save them for evolutions you want (like Pikachu → Raichu).
Heart Scales are precious — they let Pokémon relearn forgotten moves. Don't waste them on Pokémon that don't matter.
Fleeing isn't shameful. If you're unprepared for a strong enemy or a shiny, run, adjust your team, and come back — better than a full wipe.
When a shiny appears, secure the catch first. Don't attack recklessly — use sleep or paralysis to control it, whittle HP down slowly, then throw good balls. Take your time; don't kill it by accident.
When shiny hunting, always carry False Swipe or a sleep move. False Swipe leaves at least 1 HP — absolutely essential to avoid accidentally KOing a shiny.
You only get one Master Ball — save it for legendaries. Unless a super-rare shiny is about to faint, keep it for the box legendary or a difficult legendary.
Plain Poké Balls are cheap early — stock up. 50 standard balls beat 10 Ultra Balls, because standard balls work fine on low-level wilds.
Timer Balls shine in long fights. Hunting a legendary? After 10 turns the catch rate quadruples — better than an Ultra Ball.
Dusk Balls work better at night or in caves. If you explore at night, use them — cheaper and more effective than Ultra Balls.
Repeat Balls boost the catch rate for species you've already caught. When hunting for IVs or shinies of a known species, Repeat Balls are the most efficient.
Nest Balls excel against low-level Pokémon. Early game, they catch low-level wilds at a very high rate (the lower the level, the better).
Heal Balls fully restore the caught Pokémon. If you want to battle with it right away, a Heal Ball saves a trip to the Pokémon Center.
Premier Balls have no special effect — just good looks. Don't spend extra on them (unless you're a collector).
Grab good TMs early whenever you can. Thunderbolt, Flamethrower, and Surf are excellent — teach them to your mains, don't hoard them unused.
Before Gen 8, TMs were single-use. In older games (HGSS, Black/White), think carefully before teaching — once used, they're gone.
TRs in Sword/Shield are single-use. You get one shot per TR, so give them to the right Pokémon — don't waste them on HM slaves.

Don't ignore Natures entirely. You don't need to hunt them for the story, but if a Pokémon's Nature lowers its main attacking stat (like a Modest on a physical attacker), swap it or fix it later with a Mint.
During the main story, Natures barely matter. Unless you're training to high levels for the Battle Tower, don't stress over them — use who you like.
You don't need to grind EVs for the story. EVs accumulate naturally through battles and won't block your progress. Adjust them post-game with vitamins and feathers.
IVs can be completely ignored during the story. They're for post-game competitive players — newcomers need not check or breed 6V; the difference is tiny in the main plot.
Pokérus is good news, not a problem: it doubles EV gains. If you get it, spread it to your party, then box one infected Pokémon to keep it forever.
Skip breeding early. It's for late-game IV and shiny hunting — finish the story first, don't waste time on eggs.
Trade evolutions need a friend or two devices: Alakazam (Kadabra), Machamp (Machoke), Gengar (Haunter). With only one system, some of these can't evolve.
In Legends: Arceus, trade evolutions can be done solo with the Linking Cord item — the first alternative to trading, handy if you play that game.
Friendship evolutions (like Pichu → Pikachu) need walking time. Battle, avoid fainting, and feed Berries — friendship rises and evolution follows.
Don't forget held items early on: Leftovers for healing, Berries for status. Equipping your mains cuts down trips to the Pokémon Center.
Leftovers can be found mid-game. Healing 1/16 HP per turn makes it the standard for every tank — give it to your main wall as soon as you get it.
The Exp. Share is party-wide from Gen 6. In X/Y and later, everyone gains EXP, making training very easy.
In early games (Red/Blue/Green), the Exp. Share only works on one holder. Playing an old version? Remember to swap it to whoever needs levels.
Battling Pokémon gain more EXP. Even with the Exp. Share on, the one that fights earns more — so let your priority Pokémon battle most.
On level-up, Pokémon may learn new moves, and the game asks whether to replace an old one. Unsure? Decline, then relearn it later with a Heart Scale.
Evolving early isn't always better. Some unevolved forms learn moves sooner (Pikachu learns Thunder before Raichu) — delay evolution to learn powerful moves early.
Everstone blocks evolution. If you don't want a Pokémon to evolve too soon, give it an Everstone and leveling won't trigger it.
Save before Gym battles. If you lose, reload to adjust your team or grind — cheaper than losing money.
Stock up on healing items before the Elite Four. Bring at least 20 Full Restores, 10 Revives, and 10 PP items — the Elite Four is a gauntlet with no Center breaks.
PP runs low in Elite Four fights. Carry Ethers and Elixirs — don't lose your key moves mid-fight.
The Champion is usually far stronger than the Elite Four. Resupply before the Champion fight and make sure the whole team is at full health.
Save before legendary battles. If you accidentally KO a legendary, reload and try again — most don't respawn (with a few exceptions), so be careful.
For legendaries, use False Swipe down to 1 HP, then sleep or paralyze. Throw balls patiently — save the Master Ball for when you really can't catch it.
Legendaries have very low catch rates — bring dozens of balls. Stock Timer Balls, Dusk Balls, and Ultra Balls; don't run out mid-fight.
In most games, you can't re-catch a legendary — one chance only. Miss a shiny legendary and it's gone (unless you reload a save).
Roadside NPCs give useful intel. Don't rush past them — they'll tell you where rare Pokémon and items are, much faster than exploring blind.
School teachers teach the core mechanics. If you're a total newcomer, don't skip the school story — type matchups, status, and stat changes are all covered there.
Screenshot the type chart and keep it on your phone. Nobody memorizes all 18 types — check it before a Gym and you'll be fine.
STAB matters: using a move matching your Pokémon's type gives ×1.5 damage. A Charizard using Fire moves hits far harder than with Normal moves.
Super effective (×2 or ×4) matters more than STAB. Hitting the opponent's weakness doubles or quadruples damage — more effective than grinding levels.
Resistances (×0.5, ×0.25) and immunity (×0) are equally crucial. If you're at a type disadvantage, switching to a resisting or immune Pokémon saves you.
Among statuses, sleep and freeze are the strongest — they fully stop actions. Paralysis and burn are next (Speed or Attack down), and poison is weakest (unless Toxic).
Burn not only chips HP but halves physical damage. If your physical attacker gets burned, use a Burn Heal immediately — its damage is cut in half otherwise.
Paralysis quarters Speed. If your Pokémon's Speed is crippled and it's not a tank, consider a Paralyze Heal.
Toxic is terrifying in long fights — the damage doubles every turn. In drawn-out battles (like legendary catches), Toxic kills fast — cure it in time.
Confusion can betray you: 33% chance to hit yourself. Consecutive self-hits can cause surprise KOs — use a Confusion cure when you can.
Move priority decides order: Quick Attack and Extreme Speed (+1 or +2) always go first regardless of Speed. Critical for clutch kills.
Protect blocks one attack — great for stalling turns so Timer Balls gain power while catching legendaries, or buying time to heal.
Substitute absorbs a hit. Against heavy hitters, set up a Substitute to survive, then grind them down — the steady player's choice.
Baton Pass transfers stat boosts to your next Pokémon. Boost with Dragon Dance, then Baton Pass to a teammate who inherits everything — a classic strategy.
Status moves are valuable in the story. Don't run all attacks: Swords Dance (+2 Attack) and Dragon Dance (+1 Attack +1 Speed) can sweep entire teams.
Healing moves are practical too: Soft-Boiled, Moonlight, and Rest heal in battle, saving item usage — especially useful in the Elite Four.
In doubles, watch ally positioning — moves like Earthquake and Surf can hit your own partner. Read move descriptions before using them.
In doubles, protection moves matter more than Protect itself — spread moves are everywhere, and a well-timed protect saves your partner.
Weather shapes battles: rain buffs Water, sun buffs Fire, sandstorm boosts Rock's Sp. Def, and hail (now snow) boosts Ice's Defense. Late-game players learn to exploit it.
Terrain arrived in Gen 7: Electric Terrain (blocks sleep), Psychic Terrain (blocks priority), Grassy Terrain (heals + buffs Grass), Misty Terrain (blocks status). Adjust tactics accordingly.
Items in battle go beyond healing: Focus Sash saves lives, Life Orb adds damage, Assault Vest boosts Sp. Def. The right item makes a real difference.
Focus Sash keeps 1 HP from a fatal hit at full health. Crucial in tough fights — it buys one more turn. Give it to your core attacker.
Choice Band/Specs/Scarf boost damage or Speed but lock you into one move. Be careful — a locked move against a resisting opponent is a bad spot.
Weakness Policy raises Attack and Sp. Atk when hit super effectively. On a bulky Pokémon, getting countered becomes a chance to counter back.
Eviolite on an unevolved Pokémon boosts both defenses by 50%. Give it to Chansey and it becomes bulkier than its evolution Blissey — try this niche build.
Gender affects Attract and Captivate. Facing those moves? Swap in the opposite gender to dodge them (rare in the story, so don't worry too much).
Nicknames have no battle effect. Name them anything — it's pure personal taste.
Pokédex completion can wait until after the story. No rush to catch everything during the plot — go back and fill it later.
Trading gets you version exclusives. Playing Violet but want an Iron Hands? Trade with a friend or transfer via Pokémon HOME.
Pokémon HOME transfers Pokémon across generations. Played older games? Move your Pokémon from Sword/Shield to Scarlet/Violet via HOME (with some restrictions).
Event Pokémon are time-limited. Watch official announcements — shiny legendaries and rare mythicals come and go; miss one and it may be gone for years.
Events are usually claimed via Mystery Gift in-game. You'll need internet, sometimes a serial code, or a linked Pokémon HOME account.
Limited-time raids rotate regularly in Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet. Tera Raids feature special Pokémon (like Cinderace, Greninja) — miss one and you may wait months.
PVP is not required to beat the game. Don't want to fight other players? Skip it entirely — even the Battle Tower doesn't need PVP.
If you do want PVP, finish the story first. Post-game gives you high levels and full movepools — then study Natures, IVs, EVs, and team building. Don't jump in early.
Rental teams let you battle with other players' teams. In Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet, you can rent tournament-ready teams without raising them yourself.
Base stats define a Pokémon's role: high Speed for fast attackers, high HP and defenses for tanks, high Attack or Sp. Atk for cannons. Match moves to the right Pokémon.
Base stats are listed in the Pokédex and online. Arcanine has high Attack and Speed — give it physical moves; Gardevoir has high Sp. Atk and Sp. Def — give it special moves.
Check the move icons from Gen 7: orange burst = physical, blue swirl = special. Don't teach physical moves to special attackers.
Status move icons are gray or white: no direct damage, but they boost, heal, and control — don't underestimate them.
Higher power isn't everything — check accuracy. Fire Blast has 110 power but 85% accuracy; Flamethrower has 90 power and 100% accuracy — far more reliable.
100%-accuracy moves are usually the safe pick. Unless you're holding Wide Lens or Zoom Lens, don't gamble on risky moves like Thunder (70% accuracy).
The level cap is 100 in every version, but level 60-70 is plenty for the Elite Four — no need to grind to 100.
EXP Candies speed up late-game leveling. In Sword/Shield and Scarlet/Violet, raids drop plenty of candies — much faster than manual grinding.

In 2014, Twitch Plays Pokémon let tens of thousands of viewers control one Game Boy through chat commands — it took 16 days to beat Pokémon Red and spawned memes like "Praise Helix", becoming the most famous social experiment in streaming history.

The most famous urban legend of Gen 1: "Mew is under the truck". Countless players tried to push the truck near the S.S. Anne with Surf. It turned out to be a hoax, but it became the earliest "hidden content" hunt in players' memories.
MissingNo. from Gen 1: triggered by a specific NPC interaction, encountering it duplicated the sixth item in your bag by 128 — the classic way players stockpiled Master Balls.
The red Gyarados in Gen 2 (Gold/Silver): a story-guaranteed shiny, it was the first shiny for countless players and the first time many learned that shinies even existed.

Game Boy cartridges saved with a coin battery: a dead battery meant a dead save file. Players of that era carefully tracked battery life, and "change the battery without losing your save" tutorials were passed around.
The hatching bike: to maximize egg-hatching efficiency, players mapped out circular riding routes and shared them — breeding fans turned the grind into part of the fun.
Wonder Trade (from XY): random global trades spawned the classic joke of receiving a level 5 Magikarp — and occasionally a "Santa" player trading away shiny legendaries.

In the summer of 2016, Pokémon GO launched: players flooded the streets worldwide, and some police stations even posted "don't come into the station to catch Pokémon" — the biggest offline craze in gaming history.
First Edition Pokémon TCG cards: a First Edition Charizard now sells for hundreds of thousands of dollars at auction. Cards that cost pocket change back then became a "childhood investment" legend.
Game Corner slot machines: in Gens 1–3 you exchanged coins for TMs, players built slot-machine muscle memory, and the coin-exchange window always had a line.
Cerulean Cave (Mewtwo's cave): countless players saved their only Master Ball for it, while hardcore ones reset hundreds of times with regular balls — the "capture of the century".
The save point before the Elite Four: in Gen 1's Victory Road, players called the final save spot the "Gate to Heaven", because losing to the Elite Four meant restarting from there.

The following-Pokémon system in HeartGold/SoulSilver: your lead Pokémon walked behind you, and players deliberately strolled around with their shinies — the feature that helped crown it the best remake in the series.
Battle Tower BP grinding: from Gen 3 onward, battle facilities made "grind points for items" a hardcore daily routine, and BP shop prices were the talk of the community.
Pokémon Center queue culture in Japan: limited distribution events drew overnight lines, and distributed Pokémon (like Mythicals) became a generation's prized collection.

The shiny hunter community: from 1/8192 in Gen 2 to 1/4096 today, shiny hunters share strategies like chaining, hatching, and soft-resetting — some grind tens of thousands of encounters for one shiny.
Game Boy link cables: trading and trade evolutions (like Gengar and Machamp) required meeting face-to-face with a link cable — the essential social ritual of that era.
Surfing Pikachu: an officially distributed Pikachu with a special move, later immortalized in minigames and the anime — the most famous "legit exclusive move".
Pokémon Crystal introduced the first playable female protagonist, but she only appeared in that one game before being replaced — an early "cast change" moment in the series.
Many players' first Gen 1 experience came from bootleg cartridges with famously bad translations, which became beloved community memes; official Chinese localization only arrived with Sun & Moon.
Gold and Silver Bottle Caps: training items since Gen 6 — a Gold Cap maxes all six IVs to 31, a Silver Cap maxes one; using caps to fix IVs on wild high-level legendaries is standard practice.
Mints change the stat modifiers, not the nature itself: you can fix a bad nature for battle with a mint, but breeding still inherits the original nature.
Ability Capsules switch between regular abilities; the rarer Ability Patch switches to the hidden ability — only meaningful once the hidden ability is unlocked.
The Destiny Knot: a parent holding it passes down 5 of the parents' 12 IVs to offspring — the core item for breeding 6IV Pokémon.
The Everstone: a parent holding one passes its nature to offspring 100% of the time. Lock the nature first, then breed for IVs — the standard flow.
Flame Body: the ability (or Magma Armor) halves egg-hatching steps for the whole party — mandatory for breeding fans.
Masuda Method: breeding Pokémon from different language regions boosts shiny odds 6×; combined with the Shiny Charm it reaches 1/512 — the mainstream shiny-hunting method.
There is usually only one Master Ball per playthrough: deciding who gets it is an art, and the community consensus is to save it for hard-to-catch Mythicals.

Special Poké Balls have bonuses: the Heavy Ball works better on heavy Pokémon, the Love Ball on opposite-gender same-species, the Fast Ball on fast-fleeing ones — matching balls is a collector's hobby.
Hidden Abilities: wild Pokémon usually only have regular abilities; hidden ones mainly come from Max Raid battles, special dens, or event distributions.
The Eviolite: unevolved Pokémon holding it gain +50% Defense and Sp. Def, making some unevolved forms stronger in battle than their evolutions.
Choice items: the Choice Scarf locks your move but grants +50% Speed; Choice Specs/Band boost offenses at the same cost. Reading when the opponent switches is Battle 101.
Leftovers: heals 1/16 max HP every turn, the universal item forever tied to toxic stall strategies — one of the best-value items in the series.
4× type weaknesses: type multipliers stack up to 4× (e.g. Rock/Ground takes 4× from Water and Grass). Check the 4× weakness first when teambuilding.
Weather teams: rain, sun, sand, and snow each have core members and ability synergy (like Drizzle and Drought) — building a weather team is a classic competitive archetype.
Trick Room: for 5 turns speed is reversed, making slow, hard-hitting Pokémon absolute cores in Trick Room teams.
Intimidate: lowers the opponent's Attack one stage on entry — one of the most common and practical abilities; intimidate pivoting is a doubles staple.
Priority moves: Quick Attack, Extreme Speed and other +1/+2 priority moves ignore speed and always strike first — essential for revenge kills and cleanup.
Terrain effects: Electric Terrain blocks sleep, Psychic Terrain blocks priority, Grassy Terrain heals, Misty Terrain blocks status — core mechanics of the competitive scene since Gen 8.
Terastallization (Scarlet/Violet): turns a Pokémon into a single Tera type, rewriting both offensive and defensive typing — the biggest variable in Gen 9 battles.
Dynamax (Sword/Shield): for three turns HP doubles and moves become Max Moves with extra effects; Max Airstream's Speed boost defined the Gen 8 meta.
Regional forms: Alolan, Galarian, Hisuian and Paldean forms change type and appearance — the same Pokédex number in different forms is a collector's nightmare.
Friendship and Affection are separate systems: Friendship affects evolutions and Return, while Affection (from XY) affects battle luck like critical hits and surviving KOs.
Exp. Candies: since Gen 8 you can level up directly with candies, skipping the grind — but candy-only training skips EV management.
EV limits: 510 total EVs with a maximum of 252 per stat, meaning at most two stats can be maxed — the common "252/252/4" spread exists for this reason.
A wild 6IV Pokémon appears at roughly 1 in 1 billion odds: real 6IVs come from Destiny Knot breeding or Bottle Caps — don't expect to find one in the wild.
Pokérus: a rare positive virus that doubles EV gains and spreads through the party; after being cured the Pokémon keeps an immunity mark but can no longer spread it — a collector's lucky charm.
The Exp. Share became party-wide from Gen 6: no more swap-training, though some players criticized it for making the games too easy.
The Dream Ball: originally from Gen 5's Dream World, now mainly used to catch hidden-ability Pokémon — and a favorite of ball-matching collectors.
Victory Road: the final gauntlet of every mainline game, followed by the Elite Four and Champion — a team must cover many types; the traditional final exam for any trained team.
